subject: biology
title: A4.2 Conservation of biodiversity
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: A4.2 Conservation of biodiversity — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic A4.2.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering A4.2 Conservation of biodiversity, guide topic A4.2.
final_note: You worked through A4.2 Conservation of biodiversity — 8 guide statements.

concepts.def: The variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations. It includes ecosystem diversity (the range of ecosystems in a region or on Earth), species diversity (the number of species and their relative abundance) and genetic diversity (the variety of alleles within a species).

The variety of ecosystems in an area, each with its own community of species and abiotic environment. A coastline with coral reef, mangrove, seagrass meadow and lowland rainforest has higher ecosystem diversity than one with rainforest alone, and losing any one of these ecosystems reduces biodiversity even if no species is lost.

The number of species in a community (species richness) together with the relative abundance of each species (species evenness). A community dominated by one species has lower species diversity than a community in which the same species are present in similar numbers.

The variety of alleles within a species or population. High genetic diversity gives a population more scope to adapt to changing conditions and resist disease. A species can persist while losing genetic diversity: the cheetah survives as a species, but its individuals are so genetically alike that skin grafts between unrelated animals are not rejected.

A species that has been discovered, given a binomial name and formally described in a publication. Around two million species have been described, but estimates of the total number of species on Earth are several times higher, so many more species remain to be discovered, especially among insects, fungi and microorganisms. Fossil evidence suggests that more species are alive today than at any time in the past.

Terms for taxonomists who classify the same observations in different ways. A splitter treats small but consistent differences as grounds for recognizing separate species and so recognizes more species in a group; a lumper treats the same differences as variation within a species and so recognizes fewer. Neither is simply wrong: classification is pattern recognition, and the same observations can be classified in different ways (NOS).

The current episode of species extinction, in which the rate of extinction is far above the background rate estimated from the fossil record. Unlike the five earlier mass extinctions, whose causes were non-anthropogenic, its causes are human activities: hunting and other over-exploitation, destruction of habitat, pollution and the spread of pests, diseases and invasive alien species.

A flightless bird of New Zealand, the females standing up to about 2 m tall, which had evolved with no mammalian predators, matured slowly and laid few eggs. Polynesian settlers arrived around 1300 CE, hunted moa for meat, took their eggs and burned areas of forest; the species was extinct within about two centuries. It is the guide's example of the anthropogenic loss of terrestrial megafauna.

A seal of the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico, killed by Europeans from the 1490s for the oil in its blubber and for its meat and skin; later, its remaining colonies were disturbed by coastal settlement and its fish prey depleted by fishing. The last confirmed sighting was in 1952 and it was declared extinct in 2008. It is the guide's example of the anthropogenic extinction of a marine species.

A North American bird whose flocks numbered in the billions in the early 1800s. Commercial hunting for meat, made possible by the railway and the telegraph, together with the clearance of the eastern forests in which it nested, drove it to extinction; the last individual died in Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. It shows that even an extremely abundant species can be driven to extinction by anthropogenic causes. (A third case study from an area familiar to students is required; this is a widely taught example, and a local one may be substituted.)

The destruction or degradation of an ecosystem so that its characteristic community and processes disappear, even if some organisms or tree cover remain. Causes may be directly anthropogenic, such as clearance for agriculture or urbanization, or indirectly anthropogenic, such as fires that spread through land that logging and drainage have made flammable.

The lowland rainforest of Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, dominated by tall trees of the family Dipterocarpaceae. It has been lost through logging for hardwood timber, followed by clearance and burning to create oil palm and pulpwood plantations, with fires during droughts spreading through logged and drained land. It is the guide's compulsory case study of ecosystem loss in Southeast Asia.

An inland sea in Central Asia whose ecosystem was lost when, from the 1960s, the rivers feeding it were diverted to irrigate cotton and other crops. The sea shrank to a fraction of its former area and split into separate basins, its salinity rose several-fold, its fishery collapsed as the native fish species disappeared from the sea, and the exposed seabed became a salt desert from which dust and salt storms spread. It is a directly anthropogenic ecosystem loss. (A second case study from an area familiar to students is required by the guide if possible; this is a widely taught example, and a local one may be substituted.)

The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, an intergovernmental body that assesses published evidence on the state of biodiversity. Its 2019 Global Assessment concluded that around one million species are threatened with extinction and that nature is declining at rates unprecedented in human history.

The number of different species present in a community or area. It records nothing about how abundant each species is, so two surveys can record the same richness while the community has changed greatly.

How evenly the individuals in a community are distributed among the species present. A community in which most individuals belong to one species has low evenness, even when its species richness is high. Evidence of change in richness or evenness requires surveys repeated over time using the same method.

The collection of scientific data by members of the public rather than professional scientists, for example in national garden-bird or butterfly counts. It allows surveys over far larger areas and longer periods than scientists alone could cover, but brings methodological concerns: variable identification skill, uneven sampling effort and non-random choice of sites, which must be accounted for before the data are used as evidence (NOS).

Evidence that others can check. To be verifiable, evidence usually has to come from a published source that has been peer-reviewed (examined by independent experts before publication) and that describes its methodology in enough detail for the work to be checked or repeated (NOS).

Harvesting a species faster than its population can replace itself, by hunting, fishing or collecting. Hunting and other forms of over-exploitation are among the specific causes of the current biodiversity crisis.

A species carried by human activity to a region outside its natural range, where it establishes, spreads and harms native species by predation, competition or disease. Global transport, for example in ships' ballast water or with traded goods, spreads invasive alien species and also pests and diseases; this spread is one of the specific causes of the biodiversity crisis.

Conservation of species in their natural habitats, for example through the management of nature reserves. It keeps species within the ecological interactions and selection pressures of their own environment and conserves the habitat along with the species. Management is active: controlling invasive species, regulating grazing or fire, and maintaining corridors between reserves.

Conservation of species away from their natural habitat, in zoos, botanic gardens and seed or tissue banks. It protects individuals and germ plasm from threats in the wild and allows captive breeding for reintroduction, but it does not conserve the habitat, holds limited genetic diversity and cannot by itself secure a species' future.

Restoring natural processes to an area so that the ecosystem becomes self-sustaining with less need for continuing management, often by reintroducing species that had been lost, such as large herbivores or predators, and by removing barriers to their movement.

Restoring an ecosystem that has been damaged or destroyed, for example by replanting cleared forest, re-flooding drained wetland or removing pollutants from a river, so that native communities can re-establish.

Living genetic material, such as seeds, pollen, spores, cultured tissue, sperm, eggs or embryos, stored so that a species' genes are preserved. Seed banks store dried seeds at low temperature; tissue banks store cultured tissue or frozen cells, and are needed for species whose seeds cannot survive drying and freezing. Different species therefore require different measures.

A conservation programme, run by the Zoological Society of London, that prioritizes species which are both Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered. The rationale is that losing a species with few close living relatives removes a disproportionate amount of unique evolutionary history from the tree of life, and that such species are often overlooked by conservation focused on well-known animals.

A measure of how much unique evolutionary history a species represents, based on the length of the branches of the phylogenetic tree that it shares with few or no other living species. A species with no close living relatives, such as the aye-aye, has high evolutionary distinctiveness; a species in a large group of close relatives has low. It is not a measure of how old or how 'primitive' a species is.

A species' risk of extinction, taken in the EDGE programme from its IUCN Red List category, from Least Concern through Near Threatened, Vulnerable and Endangered to Critically Endangered. Combining it with evolutionary distinctiveness gives the EDGE priority; deciding which species to prioritize also has ethical, political, social, cultural and economic implications that need to be debated (NOS).

mcqs.q: A survey of an island records three findings: the island contains six distinct ecosystems; 420 species have been identified; and its population of one lizard species carries 18 alleles at a studied gene, compared with 4 alleles in the same species on a neighbouring island. Which of these findings describe the island's biodiversity?
options: All three of the findings, because biodiversity includes ecosystem, species and genetic diversity
Only the count of 420 species, because biodiversity means the variety of species
The six ecosystems and 420 species, but not the alleles, which are variation within a species
The 420 species and the 18 alleles, but not the ecosystems, which are only habitats
mcqs.specStatementText: Biodiversity is variety at three levels
mcqs.explain: Biodiversity is the variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations. The six ecosystems are ecosystem diversity, the 420 species are species diversity and the 18 alleles are genetic diversity, so all three findings describe the island's biodiversity.
rationales: Biodiversity is the variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations. The six ecosystems are ecosystem diversity, the 420 species are species diversity and the 18 alleles are genetic diversity, so all three findings describe the island's biodiversity.

A student who carries over the GCSE definition of biodiversity as the variety of species picks this. Species diversity is one level of biodiversity; the variety of ecosystems and the variety of alleles within a species are the other two.

A student who treats biodiversity as differences between species picks this. Genetic diversity, the variety of alleles within a species, is a level of biodiversity in its own right, and the lizard population with 18 alleles is more diverse than the one with 4.

A student who sees ecosystems as the setting for biodiversity rather than part of it picks this. Ecosystem diversity is the third level: a region with six distinct ecosystems holds more biodiversity than one with a single ecosystem, even with the same species.

mcqs.q: Cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus) show extremely little genetic variation: unrelated cheetahs are so alike that skin grafts between them are not rejected. In a reserve, cheetah numbers have been stable for 20 years, and the species present and their relative abundances have not changed. Which statement about biodiversity in the reserve is correct?
options: Species diversity is low, because all the cheetahs are genetically almost identical
The cheetah's genetic diversity is low, although the reserve's species diversity is unchanged
The cheetahs' uniformity does not affect biodiversity, because the number of species present is unchanged
The cheetah's genetic diversity must be adequate, because its population has been stable
mcqs.specStatementText: Biodiversity is variety at three levels
mcqs.explain: The two levels are separate. Genetic diversity is the variety of alleles within a species, and the cheetah's is extremely low; species diversity depends on the species present and their abundance, which the stem says are unchanged.
rationales: A student who thinks biodiversity has only one level, the number of species, picks this: with no genetic level to assign it to, the cheetah's uniformity gets labelled as low species diversity, conflating the genetic and species levels. Genetic uniformity within one species is low genetic diversity; species diversity concerns the number and relative abundance of species, which have not changed.

The two levels are separate. Genetic diversity is the variety of alleles within a species, and the cheetah's is extremely low; species diversity depends on the species present and their abundance, which the stem says are unchanged.

A student who does not count within-species variation as biodiversity picks this. Genetic diversity is one of the three levels, so a reserve whose cheetahs carry very few alleles holds less biodiversity than one whose cheetahs are genetically varied, whatever the species count.

A student who judges diversity by numbers picks this. Population size and genetic diversity are different things: a population can remain stable for decades while carrying very few alleles, which is exactly the cheetah's situation.

mcqs.q: Two taxonomists study the same collection of ground beetles. One recognizes 12 species. The other recognizes 4 species, treating the small differences in colour and size that separate the other taxonomist's species as variation within a species. Which statement about this situation is correct?
options: The 12-species count shows that the collection holds three times the biodiversity found by the other taxonomist
Only one of the counts can be valid, because the number of species in the collection is an objective fact
The count that matches published lists must be right, since nearly all beetle species are already described
The first taxonomist is a splitter and the second a lumper; both are valid classifications
mcqs.specStatementText: More species now than ever, and most are still undescribed
mcqs.explain: Splitters recognize more species than lumpers in a taxonomic group. The same observations have been classified in different ways, which the guide gives as an example of the nature of science: classification is pattern recognition, not a fixed fact.
rationales: A student who equates biodiversity with the species count picks this. The beetles are the same organisms with the same variation whichever way they are classified; only the number of names has changed, not the biodiversity of the collection.

A student who treats a species count as a measurement picks this. Classification is pattern recognition, and how much difference counts as a species boundary is a judgement; the same observations can be classified in different ways.

A student who sees classification as finished picks this. A published list is itself the product of earlier splitting or lumping decisions, and many beetle species remain undescribed, so no list settles how much consistent difference marks a species boundary; both classifications are valid.

Splitters recognize more species than lumpers in a taxonomic group. The same observations have been classified in different ways, which the guide gives as an example of the nature of science: classification is pattern recognition, not a fixed fact.

mcqs.q: Polynesian settlers reached New Zealand around 1300 CE. Within about two centuries the North Island giant moa (Dinornis novaezealandiae), a flightless bird that had evolved with no mammalian predators, matured slowly and laid few eggs, was extinct. Archaeological sites contain large numbers of butchered moa bones and moa eggshell. Which explanation of the extinction is best supported?
options: Hunting of adults and taking of eggs, with burning of forest, removed moa faster than a slow-breeding population could replace them
A natural shift in climate at the time, of the kind behind earlier mass extinctions, removed the moa independently of the settlers
Rats and dogs brought by the settlers ate the eggs, since a few thousand people with stone tools could not hunt out so big a bird
Hunting can be ruled out because moa were abundant when the settlers arrived, so loss of forest to fire must be the only cause
mcqs.specStatementText: Humans are causing the sixth mass extinction
mcqs.explain: The butchery sites show intensive hunting; a species that matured slowly, laid few eggs and had no defensive behaviour against predators could not replace the losses, and burning of forest reduced its habitat. This is the guide's example of anthropogenic loss of terrestrial megafauna.
rationales: The butchery sites show intensive hunting; a species that matured slowly, laid few eggs and had no defensive behaviour against predators could not replace the losses, and burning of forest reduced its habitat. This is the guide's example of anthropogenic loss of terrestrial megafauna.

A student who assumes extinctions have natural causes picks this. The moa had survived many climate shifts over millions of years and vanished within two centuries of human arrival, with the butchery sites showing what removed it.

A student who thinks extinction needs industrial scale picks this. The evidence of butchered bones points to hunting by people, and a small population can exterminate a slow-breeding species that does not flee from predators, because removal only has to exceed replacement.

A student who believes abundant species are safe from hunting picks this. Abundance delays extinction but does not prevent it: the butchery sites show that hunting was central, and burning of forest added to the pressure rather than replacing it.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the Caribbean monk seal (Neomonachus tropicalis) case study is correct?
options: It became extinct only after industrial fishing fleets reached the Caribbean in the twentieth century
It was hunted for the oil in its blubber from the 1490s, an anthropogenic extinction of a marine mammal species
It shows that marine species are otherwise safe, since the open ocean is too large for people to affect them
Its extinction counts as anthropogenic only because seals were killed; the fishing of its prey was a natural pressure
mcqs.specStatementText: Humans are causing the sixth mass extinction
mcqs.explain: Europeans killed Caribbean monk seals for blubber oil, meat and skins from the 1490s; later, coastal settlement disturbed its colonies and fishing depleted its prey. The last confirmed sighting was in 1952 and it was declared extinct in 2008.
rationales: A student who links extinction with modern technology picks this. Killing of monk seals for blubber oil began in the 1490s, and the species was reduced to scattered colonies long before industrial fishing; the last confirmed sighting was in 1952.

Europeans killed Caribbean monk seals for blubber oil, meat and skins from the 1490s; later, coastal settlement disturbed its colonies and fishing depleted its prey. The last confirmed sighting was in 1952 and it was declared extinct in 2008.

A student who pictures the ocean as a refuge picks this. Marine species breed and feed at particular sites; the monk seal was killed on its beaches and its prey depleted by fishing, and it is one of many marine species threatened by human activity.

A student who counts only direct killing as a human cause picks this. Depletion of prey by fishing and disturbance of colonies by settlement are indirectly anthropogenic causes, and the guide's study of extinction includes them.

mcqs.q: Mixed dipterocarp forest once covered the lowlands of Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula. Which description of how this ecosystem has been lost is correct?
options: Conversion to oil palm has replaced one kind of forest with another, so species have been lost but the ecosystem has not
Droughts and forest fires that are unconnected with human activity have destroyed most of the lowland forest
Logging for hardwood timber, followed by clearance and burning of the land for oil palm and pulpwood plantations
The growth of cities across the lowlands, because human population growth acts on ecosystems through urbanization
mcqs.specStatementText: Whole ecosystems are being lost to human activity
mcqs.explain: Dipterocarp trees were logged for their valuable timber, and the logged forest was then cleared and burned to make way for oil palm and pulpwood plantations; fires during droughts spread through logged and drained land. All of these causes are directly or indirectly anthropogenic.
rationales: A student who takes any tree cover to be forest picks this. An oil palm plantation is a crop of one species that supports a small fraction of the forest community; the dipterocarp forest ecosystem has been lost even though trees remain.

A student who treats fire and drought as purely natural picks this. Intact dipterocarp forest rarely burns; the fires spread through forest opened by logging and peatland dried by drainage, and many are started to clear land, so the loss is indirectly anthropogenic.

Dipterocarp trees were logged for their valuable timber, and the logged forest was then cleared and burned to make way for oil palm and pulpwood plantations; fires during droughts spread through logged and drained land. All of these causes are directly or indirectly anthropogenic.

A student who equates population growth with the spread of cities picks this. Urbanization occupies little of the lowland forest; the land was taken by logging and plantation agriculture, which population growth drives through demand for timber and palm oil.

mcqs.q: A survey of a lowland region of Borneo reports the following percentages of the land area. Tree canopy cover above 60%: 82% in 1990, 74% in 2020. Mixed dipterocarp forest: 80% in 1990, 31% in 2020. Oil palm and pulpwood plantation: 1% in 1990, 42% in 2020. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
options: Little ecosystem loss has occurred, because canopy cover fell by only 8 percentage points and most of the region still carries trees
The forest was lost mainly to drought and fire, which are natural events and so do not count as anthropogenic ecosystem loss
Human population growth explains the loss through the spread of settlements, since urban land must account for the difference
Canopy cover understates the loss, because plantations keep tree cover but are not the forest ecosystem
mcqs.specStatementText: Whole ecosystems are being lost to human activity
mcqs.explain: Forest fell by 49 percentage points while canopy cover fell by only 8, and plantation rose by 41. Most of the cleared forest became plantation with a closed canopy, so a measure of tree cover hides the loss of the mixed dipterocarp ecosystem.
rationales: A student who equates tree cover with forest picks this. Canopy cover changed little because plantations replaced forest tree for tree, but the dipterocarp forest ecosystem fell from 80% to 31% of the region, a loss of 49 percentage points.

A student who separates fire from human activity picks this. The data show that the lost forest area (49 percentage points) is almost matched by the growth of plantations (41 percentage points), so the land was converted; fire used in clearing is part of that conversion.

A student who equates population growth with cities picks this. The data attribute the change to plantations, which rose by 41 percentage points; population growth is the overarching cause, acting here through demand for palm oil and timber rather than through urban land.

Forest fell by 49 percentage points while canopy cover fell by only 8, and plantation rose by 41. Most of the cleared forest became plantation with a closed canopy, so a measure of tree cover hides the loss of the mixed dipterocarp ecosystem.

mcqs.q: A woodland was surveyed for ground beetles in 2000 and again in 2020 using the same pitfall-trap method and the same trapping effort. In 2000, 8 species were caught and the most abundant species made up 20% of the individuals. In 2020, 8 species were caught and the most abundant species made up 75% of the individuals. What do these results show?
options: Species richness was unchanged but species evenness fell, a change that only a repeated survey could reveal
Biodiversity was unchanged, because both surveys recorded the same number of beetle species
The 2020 survey alone would have shown the decline, since it recorded the dominance of one species
Species diversity rose between the surveys, because the dominant species contributed many more individuals
mcqs.specStatementText: Showing the crisis needs repeated, verifiable surveys
mcqs.explain: Richness (8 species) is the same, but in 2020 one species made up three-quarters of the catch, so evenness has fallen and species diversity is lower. The change is only visible because the survey was repeated with the same method.
rationales: Richness (8 species) is the same, but in 2020 one species made up three-quarters of the catch, so evenness has fallen and species diversity is lower. The change is only visible because the survey was repeated with the same method.

A student who uses richness as the whole measure picks this. Species diversity also depends on evenness, and a community in which one species has gone from 20% to 75% of individuals has become less diverse even though every species is still present.

A student used to interpreting a single sample picks this. On its own, the 2020 survey shows only that one species is dominant; without the 2000 survey there is no evidence that this is a change rather than the woodland's normal state.

A student who judges diversity by numbers of individuals picks this. Diversity is a measure of variety, not abundance: more individuals concentrated in one species lowers evenness and therefore lowers species diversity.

mcqs.q: A national scheme asks members of the public to record every bird species seen in their garden during one hour on a chosen weekend each year. Over 10 years, the number of records of a rare species rose from 40 to 300, while the number of participants rose from 5 000 to 60 000. Which statement about this evidence is correct?
options: The species has become about seven times more common over the ten years, because its records rose from 40 to 300 sightings
Records per participant fell from 0.008 to 0.005, so the rise in records reflects effort, not evidence of an increase
The results became verifiable evidence as soon as the scheme published its yearly totals on its website
A single year's count would have shown the trend equally well, because so many people took part in the scheme
mcqs.specStatementText: Showing the crisis needs repeated, verifiable surveys
mcqs.explain: 40 ÷ 5 000 = 0.008 and 300 ÷ 60 000 = 0.005. Once the twelve-fold rise in participants is accounted for, the rate of records has fallen, so the raw totals give no evidence that the species has increased. Correcting for effort is one of the methodological concerns unique to citizen science.
rationales: A student who reads raw records as abundance picks this. Records depend on how many people are looking: 40 records from 5 000 participants is 0.008 per participant, and 300 from 60 000 is 0.005, so records per participant have fallen.

40 ÷ 5 000 = 0.008 and 300 ÷ 60 000 = 0.005. Once the twelve-fold rise in participants is accounted for, the rate of records has fallen, so the raw totals give no evidence that the species has increased. Correcting for effort is one of the methodological concerns unique to citizen science.

A student who equates 'published' with 'verifiable' picks this. To be verifiable, evidence usually has to come from a peer-reviewed source that allows the methodology, including how effort and identification were handled, to be checked.

A student who draws conclusions from a single snapshot picks this. However many people take part, one year's count gives no information about change; a trend can only be shown by repeating the survey and comparing years.

mcqs.q: Why do surveys of biodiversity need to be repeated to provide evidence for a biodiversity crisis?
options: Repeating a survey is needed only when the first survey was carried out by citizen scientists rather than experts
Repeating a survey finds additional species, and so gives a higher measure of the habitat's biodiversity
A change in species richness or evenness can only be shown by comparing surveys made at two different times
A single thorough survey is sufficient, provided that it covers a wide enough range of habitats around the world
mcqs.specStatementText: Showing the crisis needs repeated, verifiable surveys
mcqs.explain: A single survey describes a community at one moment. Evidence of a biodiversity crisis is evidence of decline, so the survey must be repeated, with the same methods, so that richness and evenness can be compared over time; reports such as those of IPBES draw on such repeated surveys.
rationales: A student who thinks expert data need no comparison picks this. Repetition is required whoever collects the data, because a single survey, however skilled, records only one point in time and cannot show change.

A student who treats richness as the whole of biodiversity picks this. The purpose of repetition is to compare the community at different times, not to lengthen the species list; evidence of a crisis is evidence of change in richness and evenness.

A single survey describes a community at one moment. Evidence of a biodiversity crisis is evidence of decline, so the survey must be repeated, with the same methods, so that richness and evenness can be compared over time; reports such as those of IPBES draw on such repeated surveys.

A student used to a single fieldwork sample picks this. Wide coverage of habitats is required, but breadth cannot substitute for time: without an earlier survey to compare with, even a global survey cannot show that biodiversity is falling.

mcqs.q: Which factor is the overarching cause of the current biodiversity crisis, driving each of the specific causes?
options: Spread of cities over natural habitat
Natural spread of invasive species
Natural climate shifts as in past eras
Growth of the human population
mcqs.explain: The guide names human population growth as the overarching cause, with hunting and over-exploitation, urbanization, deforestation and clearance for agriculture, pollution and the spread of pests, diseases and invasive alien species as the specific causes it drives.
rationales: A student who pictures population growth as the spread of cities picks this. Urbanization is one of the specific causes; the overarching cause is the growth of the human population, which drives urbanization along with every other specific cause.

A student who thinks invasive species arrive by themselves picks this. Their spread is a specific cause of the crisis, and it is due to global transport by people, not natural dispersal; it is not the overarching cause.

A student who assumes extinction has natural causes picks this. The current crisis is anthropogenic; its causes are human activities driven by population growth, not the non-anthropogenic events behind earlier mass extinctions.

The guide names human population growth as the overarching cause, with hunting and over-exploitation, urbanization, deforestation and clearance for agriculture, pollution and the spread of pests, diseases and invasive alien species as the specific causes it drives.

mcqs.q: The zebra mussel (Dreissena polymorpha), native to the Caspian and Black Sea region, was first recorded in the North American Great Lakes in 1988, having arrived in the ballast water of ships. It has since spread widely and smothers native mussels. Which statement correctly relates this case to the causes of the biodiversity crisis?
options: It is an invasive alien species whose spread is a consequence of global transport, one of the specific causes of the crisis
It reached the Great Lakes by natural range expansion, so its spread is not a human cause of biodiversity loss
Its spread results from urbanization along the lake shores, the route by which population growth affects biodiversity
Native mussels are not at risk, since populations as large as theirs cannot be eliminated by a competing species
mcqs.explain: The mussel was carried outside its natural range in ships' ballast water, established and now harms native species: an invasive alien species spread by global transport, which the guide lists among the specific causes of the biodiversity crisis.
rationales: The mussel was carried outside its natural range in ships' ballast water, established and now harms native species: an invasive alien species spread by global transport, which the guide lists among the specific causes of the biodiversity crisis.

A student who takes 'invasive' to mean self-propelled picks this. The mussel crossed an ocean in ballast water; without human transport it could not have reached the Great Lakes, so its presence is anthropogenic.

A student who equates population growth with cities picks this. The mussel arrived through shipping, which population growth drives through trade; urbanization is a separate specific cause and did not transport the mussel.

A student who believes abundant species are safe picks this. Abundance does not prevent extinction when removal exceeds replacement; native mussel populations in invaded lakes have collapsed as zebra mussels smother them.

mcqs.q: Seeds of many tropical rainforest trees are killed by the drying and freezing used in seed banks. A conservation programme wants to conserve one such tree species, whose natural forest is being logged. Which approach to conserving this species is appropriate?
options: Dry and freeze its seeds in a seed bank, because seed banks can preserve the germ plasm of any species of plant
Store its germ plasm as cultured tissue in a tissue bank, alongside protection of the remaining forest in situ
Grow the tree in a botanic garden alone, so that its natural forest habitat no longer needs to be protected
Fence off the remaining forest and leave it unmanaged, since a reserve protects a species by itself
mcqs.specStatementText: No single conservation method is enough
mcqs.explain: Species whose seeds cannot survive seed banking are conserved as tissue cultures or living plants, and because no single approach is sufficient, ex situ storage is combined with in situ conservation of the habitat. Different species require different measures.
rationales: A student who assumes all seeds can be banked picks this. The stem states that this species' seeds are killed by drying and freezing, so a seed bank would destroy the germ plasm it was meant to store.

Species whose seeds cannot survive seed banking are conserved as tissue cultures or living plants, and because no single approach is sufficient, ex situ storage is combined with in situ conservation of the habitat. Different species require different measures.

A student who treats ex situ conservation as sufficient picks this. A botanic garden holds few individuals and limited genetic diversity and does not conserve the forest ecosystem or the species' ecological role; in situ protection is still needed.

A student who thinks in situ conservation means excluding people picks this. A reserve needs active management against logging, fire and invasive species, and for a species this threatened ex situ storage of germ plasm is also needed as insurance.

mcqs.q: Which description of an approach to the conservation of biodiversity is correct?
options: Nature reserves conserve species by keeping people out, so no management is needed
Ex situ conservation in zoos can, by itself, secure the future of an endangered animal species
Rewilding restores natural processes to an area, often by reintroducing missing species
Seed banks can store the germ plasm of every plant species by drying and freezing its seeds
mcqs.specStatementText: No single conservation method is enough
mcqs.explain: Rewilding aims to make an ecosystem self-sustaining by restoring the natural processes it has lost, for example by reintroducing large herbivores or predators and removing barriers to movement; it is one of the several approaches the guide requires.
rationales: A student who thinks protection means exclusion picks this. Management of nature reserves is an approach in its own right: controlling invasive species, maintaining grazing or fire regimes and keeping corridors between reserves.

A student who sees zoos as arks picks this. Captive populations are small, may lose genetic diversity and natural behaviours, and do not conserve the habitat; no single approach by itself is sufficient.

Rewilding aims to make an ecosystem self-sustaining by restoring the natural processes it has lost, for example by reintroducing large herbivores or predators and removing barriers to movement; it is one of the several approaches the guide requires.

A student who assumes seeds are uniformly hardy picks this. Many species have seeds that are killed by drying and freezing, so their germ plasm is stored in tissue banks or as living plants; different species require different measures.

mcqs.q: The EDGE of Existence programme scores species for Evolutionary Distinctiveness (ED) and Global Endangerment (GE). Four species are assessed: W has high ED and is Critically Endangered; X has high ED and is of Least Concern; Y has low ED and is Critically Endangered; Z has low ED and is of Least Concern. Which species does the EDGE programme prioritize, and why?
options: Species Y, because the most endangered species must be conserved first, whatever its relatives
Species X, because the most distinct lineage is the oldest and should be conserved first
Species Z, because a species of Least Concern has the largest population and most genetic diversity
Species W, because it combines few close relatives with a high risk of extinction
mcqs.specStatementText: EDGE prioritizes species that are distinct and endangered
mcqs.explain: EDGE prioritizes species that are both evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered. W's loss would remove a large amount of unique evolutionary history and is likely, so it receives the highest priority.
rationales: A student who uses threat as the only criterion picks this. Y is as endangered as W, but it has many close relatives, so its loss would remove little unique evolutionary history; EDGE combines endangerment with distinctiveness.

A student who equates distinctiveness with age picks this. X is distinct but is not threatened, so it does not need priority; and distinctiveness measures unique evolutionary history, not how old a species is.
A student who judges by numbers picks this. Population size is not genetic diversity, and Z is neither threatened nor distinct, so it scores lowest on both EDGE criteria.

EDGE prioritizes species that are both evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered. W's loss would remove a large amount of unique evolutionary history and is likely, so it receives the highest priority.

mcqs.q: A conservation budget can fund a recovery programme for only one of two species: a large, well-known mammal with many close relatives that attracts tourists, or a small, little-known amphibian with no close living relatives that is Critically Endangered. Which statement about deciding between them is correct?
options: The EDGE rationale favours the amphibian, but the choice also has ethical, economic and cultural implications that need to be debated
The decision is purely scientific: the species' scores settle the matter, so there is nothing left to debate
The mammal must be chosen, because conservation effort should go to the species that people care about most
The amphibian must be chosen, because having no close relatives makes it the older and more primitive species
mcqs.specStatementText: EDGE prioritizes species that are distinct and endangered
mcqs.explain: The amphibian is evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered, so EDGE would prioritize it. The guide's NOS point is that such decisions also carry ethical, environmental, political, social, cultural and economic implications, so scores inform a debate rather than replace it.
rationales: The amphibian is evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered, so EDGE would prioritize it. The guide's NOS point is that such decisions also carry ethical, environmental, political, social, cultural and economic implications, so scores inform a debate rather than replace it.

A student who expects data to make the decision picks this. EDGE scores identify which loss would remove the most unique evolutionary history, but livelihoods from tourism, cultural value and ethics are also at stake, and the guide says such issues need to be debated.

A student who uses appeal as the criterion picks this. Popularity is one consideration in the debate, but the mammal has many close relatives and its loss would remove little unique evolutionary history; the EDGE rationale exists to stop such species crowding out distinct ones.

A student who reads distinctiveness as age picks this. The amphibian's priority under EDGE comes from the unique evolutionary history it represents and its endangerment, not from being older; and even then the decision is not automatic.

More species now than ever, and most are still undescribed
Humans are causing the sixth mass extinction
Whole ecosystems are being lost to human activity
Showing the crisis needs repeated, verifiable surveys
No single conservation method is enough
EDGE prioritizes species that are distinct and endangered

scopeNotes.howHonoured: No concept or item tests the causes of the five earlier mass extinctions as content. Earlier mass extinctions are mentioned only as the contrast in c07 and as the natural-cause belief (m08) behind distractors in q05 and q12, which are marked wrong for that reason; no key requires knowledge of asteroid impact, volcanism or past climate change.

Every cause of ecosystem loss in the bank is human in origin: logging, clearance and burning for plantations, and fires that spread through logged and drained land during droughts (treated as indirectly anthropogenic). No content covers ecosystems lost to purely natural events such as volcanic eruptions or natural sea-level change.
